dynamo.title: Try it · DynamoDB RCU/WCU calculator
dynamo.purpose: Round the item size first, then apply consistency and requests per second.
dynamo.fallback: 12 KB → 3 read-size units × 0.5 × 16 reads/s = 24 RCUs. One normal 12 KB write/s needs 12 WCUs.
dynamo.caveat: Successful single-item operations, equally sized items, no secondary-index write costs. Whole provisioned settings have a minimum of 1 RCU and 1 WCU; this is arithmetic sizing before headroom.

edge.title: Try it · CloudFront request router
edge.purpose: Trace a cache miss: path routing and primary/secondary failover are separate choices.
edge.fallback: GET /images/logo.png → CloudFront PoP → S3. /api/orders routes to ALB. With a group, an eligible failed request retries a matching backup.
edge.caveat: Assumes cache miss, allowed method and configured 503 failover; OPTIONS caching is enabled. Each path’s group has a backup serving the same content. No health probes or requests run here.

policy.title: Try it · IAM identity vs queue policy
policy.purpose: Evaluate one IAM principal and one SQS action, in the same account or across accounts.
policy.fallback: Same account: either applicable Allow can suffice. Cross-account IAM access: both sides typically allow. Applicable explicit Deny always wins.
policy.caveat: Only policies matching this principal, action, resource and conditions are toggled. Other controls are assumed satisfied: SCPs/RCPs, boundaries, session/endpoint policies and KMS can restrict access. SNS service-principal evaluation is a separate example, not modelled as an IAM role.

redis.title: Try it · Shards vs replicas
redis.purpose: One Region, node-based Redis OSS/Valkey cluster mode enabled. Each shard owns a different part of the keyspace.
redis.fallback: Three shards each have a primary and no replicas. Add shards for aggregate write/storage capacity; add replicas for reads and failover candidates.
redis.caveat: Standard node-based cache with durability mode off. Illustrative stable hash and even slot ranges, not actual Redis CRC16 placement or a real resharding/failover procedure. Nodes can span AZs; async replicas are not guaranteed zero-data-loss copies.

cache.title: Try it · REST API cache flow
cache.purpose: Assume successful API authentication; separately decide whether the caller may invalidate the cached response.
cache.fallback: Unexpired entry → cache hit. Authorised max-age=0 → backend fetch → replace entry. Unauthorised invalidation can be rejected or ignored according to configuration.
cache.caveat: Method requires authorisation for invalidation; caller’s normal invoke permission is assumed allowed. “Unexpired” describes TTL, not guaranteed source-data freshness. REST API response cache only.

alb.title: Try it · ALB frontend and target routing
alb.purpose: A public frontend can route to private targets; registering a target does not build network connectivity.
alb.fallback: Client → ALB DNS → listener → matching rule → target group → healthy target. Internal ALBs need private connectivity; private IP targets still need routes and network permissions.
alb.caveat: Assumes valid DNS, ALB listener rules/SG, NACLs and target health. IP examples use permitted private ranges. Lambda invocation permission is assumed allowed; it is not a target TCP connection.

firewall.title: Try it · Stateful SG vs stateless NACL
firewall.purpose: Model one TCP connection at the receiving subnet. The frontend and backend are separate connections.

controls.label: Target SG allows new inbound connection
Target-subnet NACL allows service destination port
Target-subnet NACL allows response ephemeral destination port

firewall.fallback: Browser:54321 → ALB:80; ALB:80 → Browser:54321. Stateful SG permits the response; stateless NACL needs an outbound destination-port rule for 54321.
firewall.caveat: Initiator-side controls/routes and target application are assumed permitted. This is ordinary tracked TCP traffic; special untracked flows are outside the exercise. Actual ephemeral ranges depend on the initiator.

metrics.title: Try it · Choose the metric source
metrics.purpose: First identify the signal; then decide whether you need a new publisher or simply faster native samples.

controls.label: Requirement
options: Scale on ALB requests per target

controls.label: This architecture has an ALB + target group

metrics.fallback: CPU → native metric. Memory → agent/custom publisher. App-specific rate → instrumentation. ALB requests/target → ALB native metric if an ALB exists. Faster EC2 native samples → detailed monitoring.
metrics.caveat: A valid metric must exist with the correct dimensions and scaling behaviour. Standard custom resolution is 60 s; high-resolution custom data uses StorageResolution=1. Detailed EC2 monitoring is normally 1 minute, not 1 second.

cache-choice.title: Try it · Choose the cache boundary
cache-choice.purpose: Choose for the deciding requirement; another technology can be technically possible with more application work.

controls.label: Requirement
options: Shared DynamoDB products · least cache logic
Latest committed DynamoDB data · strong read

cache-choice.fallback: DAX simplifies eligible DynamoDB read caching; Redis supports general-purpose cached values; CloudFront serves cacheable HTTP content. Strong reads bypass cached copies.
cache-choice.caveat: Choices describe a typical fit, not exclusive technical possibilities. Session durability/expiry and tenant-level authorisation still need application design.

invocation.title: Try it · Find the failing permission hop
invocation.purpose: Select a stage, then test caller, integration and execution permissions independently.

controls.label: Selected Lambda resource policy permits API Gateway
Configured API Gateway invocation role is trusted + permits InvokeFunction
Lambda execution role permits required DynamoDB action

invocation.fallback: Client → API authorisation → Gateway invoke permission → Lambda → execution-role permission → DynamoDB. A stage variable selects the function; it grants no access.
invocation.caveat: Same-account illustration, no explicit Deny, valid integration/alias/source-ARN scopes. The role toggle means the alternative integration credentials role is correctly configured. Other IAM controls are assumed satisfied.

cli.title: Try it · CLI projection, filtering and pagination
cli.purpose: Use Users for attributes/filters, or switch to 250 S3 objects to see 100 → 100 → 50 output pages.
cli.fallback: Users: --page-size 4 and --max-items 5 can require two underlying calls. Projection/filtering change output, not the cost of evaluating the same records. The CLI NextToken resumes with --starting-token.
cli.caveat: Fixed illustrative dataset order; actual DynamoDB Scan order is not guaranteed. Service pages are below 1 MB. Cursor handling is simplified, including intra-page resume; tokens are simulated and never sent to AWS. Changing dataset resets options/tokens.

fifo.title: Try it · FIFO group order vs duplicate sends
fifo.purpose: Send two users’ operations, receive their group heads, and compare retries before and after five minutes.

controls.label: Generate deduplication ID from body instead

fifo.fallback: Per-user groups can progress independently. Reusing a send deduplication ID inside five minutes is acknowledged without adding another deliverable message, even after the first is deleted.
fifo.caveat: Queue-wide deduplication scope, one active head per group and successful DeleteMessage on completion. Content-hash equality is simulated; real SQS uses SHA-256 of body, excluding attributes. An explicit ID overrides content-based generation in real SQS.

gsi.title: Try it · GSI capacity and write back-pressure
gsi.purpose: Compare base-table writes with the additional index-entry writes and eventual index reads.

controls.label: GSI entry size · KB (keys + projected attributes)

gsi.fallback: 100 new 3 KB items/s need 300 table WCUs. One 1.5 KB GSI entry per item adds 200 index WCUs; a 150-WCU index can back-pressure table writes. Forty eventual index reads/s use 20 RCUs at this size.
gsi.caveat: Provisioned mode, one GSI, successful new eligible items, one index write per base write, no changed index keys/transactions or burst/adaptive headroom. Each Query evaluates/retrieves one projected entry; multi-entry Query size aggregation differs. KB = 1,024 bytes. It is sizing arithmetic, not an exact throttle predictor.

cutover.title: Try it · Replacement deployment cutover
cutover.purpose: Compare the gap with no ready server, stable-IP reassociation, and independent-server redundancy.
cutover.fallback: Prepare-and-move EIP keeps one public IPv4 address but may briefly interrupt traffic. DNS redundancy uses different endpoints and has detection/caching considerations.
cutover.caveat: Qualitative comparison only; no universal downtime seconds are claimed. EIPs are regional public IPv4 addresses. A redundant authoritative DNS design differs from simply changing an A record.

cache-key.title: Try it · CloudFront language cache key
cache-key.purpose: Request English, then Japanese, before and after including lang in the cache key.
cache-key.fallback: Without lang in the key, /reviews?lang=en can populate /reviews, and a later lang=jp request hits the English response. Including lang separates variants.
cache-key.caveat: One edge cache, unexpired entries, origin returns the requested language. In both modes the origin receives lang (via cache/origin-request policy); this isolates the cache-key mistake. Changing policy does not clear this local model’s previous entries.

kcl.title: Try it · KCL shard leases and workers
kcl.purpose: A worker can own several shard leases; extra workers do not create more shards.
kcl.fallback: Ten shards and twenty one-worker instances → ten active workers and ten without shard leases within one application. Each independent application has its own lease/checkpoint set.
kcl.caveat: Even, settled lease assignment; one KCL worker per instance is an assumption, not an EC2 rule. Real balancing/recovery is dynamic. Multiple applications still share normal read limits unless using eligible dedicated fan-out.

kms-cache.title: Try it · KMS data-key request counter
kms-cache.purpose: Compare fresh materials per transaction with deliberately bounded reuse in one eligible cache.

controls.label: Illustrative messages per cached data key

kms-cache.fallback: 1,000 encryptions: fresh data keys ≈1,000 GenerateDataKey calls; batches of 100 eligible messages ≈10 calls. Real age, byte, context and cache-miss rules can refresh sooner.
kms-cache.caveat: Illustrative ceiling(transactions / reuse), not the exact Encryption SDK threshold algorithm. No cryptography, nonce generation, decryption calls or AWS requests run. Protect cached plaintext materials, retain unique required IV/nonces, and configure age/message/byte security limits.

cache-strategy.title: Try it · Lazy load, write-through or invalidate
cache-strategy.purpose: Read first, write an updated value, then read again; compare the cache and database.

controls.label: Simulate cache set/delete failure after DB commit

cache-strategy.fallback: Lazy+TTL: read $100, update DB to $120, then an unexpired cache can still return $100. TTL expiry does not refresh it; the next read fetches $120. Write-through updates; invalidation deletes.
cache-strategy.caveat: One item, serial calls; changing item/strategy resets the example. Write-through/invalidation are shown synchronously, but can also be asynchronous. Separate DB/cache calls and concurrent readers need stronger controls for strict freshness.

endpoint.title: Try it · Private-subnet service access
endpoint.purpose: Assume EC2 has no public IP, NAT or IGW path; choose the endpoint mechanism and its configuration.

controls.label: Gateway route associated with application subnet
Interface endpoint SG permits HTTPS source
Use private DNS or endpoint-specific DNS

endpoint.fallback: EC2 → S3/DynamoDB gateway endpoint uses a service-prefix-list route, not an endpoint ENI. Secrets Manager/KMS use supported interface endpoints with private ENIs and security groups.
endpoint.caveat: Same-Region standard connectivity; EC2 egress SG, NACLs, normal local routing, IAM/resource/endpoint policies are assumed permitted. S3 and DynamoDB also support interface endpoints. The service itself remains regional, outside the customer subnet.

s3-access.title: Try it · EC2 credentials vs S3 bucket access
s3-access.purpose: Detach the role and expire its cached credentials separately; inspect GetObject and PutObject.

controls.label: Bucket permits public / anonymous GetObject (BPA permits)
Role detached; profile change has propagated
Previously issued role credentials still valid

s3-access.fallback: Detachment stops ongoing credential supply after propagation, not every already-issued credential. A separate public bucket read grant can still allow GetObject; an explicit PutObject Deny wins.
s3-access.caveat: Existing role remains defined with the selected policies; it is detached, not deleted. Public read is a hypothetical independently allowed path, not a recommendation. Named-principal bucket grants need valid matching credentials. Other IAM/BPA/network controls are assumed satisfied; no five-minute grace is modelled. Objects in this access-only model have no extra KMS decryption requirement.

trace.title: Try it · X-Ray annotation vs metadata
trace.purpose: Enrich one sampled trace, search its indexed annotation, then try searching metadata.
trace.fallback: Annotations are indexed scalar labels; metadata can hold nested debugging data but is not an indexed X-Ray filter. DynamoDB appears through an instrumented client subsegment/inferred node.
trace.caveat: Deterministic illustrative batch of 20 requests; generate a new batch to apply the chosen sampling rate. This is not the default reservoir algorithm. No real traces are emitted; avoid putting sensitive values in telemetry.

s3-key.title: Try it · Follow the S3 encryption key
s3-key.purpose: Compare the direction of object data, a KMS key identifier and an actual customer-supplied key.
s3-key.fallback: SSE-S3: S3 manages keys. SSE-KMS: S3 uses KMS-protected data keys. SSE-C: client supplies actual key over HTTPS; S3 encrypts and does not retain it. SSE-C does not inherently use KMS.
s3-key.caveat: All three encrypt on S3’s side. HTTPS is recommended throughout and mandatory for SSE-C. Bucket policies/key permissions and the current default SSE-C block still apply; this selector performs no encryption.

review.title: LSI vs GSI
review.question: An existing Orders table needs a new OrderStatus partition-key lookup. Which index can be added?

options.text: LSI
options.why: LSIs must be created with the table and share its partition key.

options.text: GSI
options.why: A GSI can be added later with another partition key; existing eligible items are backfilled.

options.text: Either index
options.why: Creation timing and partition-key rules differ.

review.analogy: A new catalogue can use a new filing system; a local drawer keeps its existing key.

review.title: Shard vs stream capacity
review.question: Ten provisioned shards receive 5 MiB/s, but one gets 4 MiB/s. What explains write throttling?

options.text: The stream has no spare capacity
options.why: The theoretical aggregate byte budget is 10 MiB/s, but it is not a shared pool.

options.text: One shard exceeds its sustained write budget
options.why: A shard is limited to 1 MiB/s and 1,000 records/s. Key skew can overload it despite idle shards.

options.text: Consumers deleted the shard
options.why: Reads do not delete Kinesis records or shards.

review.analogy: Empty checkout lanes do not lend their capacity to one overloaded lane.

review.title: Kinesis exceptions
review.question: Which interpretation best distinguishes these errors?

options.text: LimitExceededException always means a hot shard
options.why: It typically concerns service quotas/control-plane limits; inspect the operation.

options.text: Both mean the same thing
options.why: Throughput pressure and service/API quota pressure need different investigation.

options.text: ProvisionedThroughputExceededException indicates data-plane throughput pressure
options.why: Investigate shard write/read limits for the failing operation; LimitExceededException typically concerns service or control-plane limits.

review.analogy: A busy checkout lane differs from the store’s limit on opening new lanes.

review.title: Eventual read arithmetic
review.question: A 12 KB item is read 16 times/s using eventual consistency. What steady read capacity does this require before headroom?

options.text: 24 RCUs
options.why: ceil(12/4) × 0.5 × 16 = 24 RCUs. Eventual reads consume half the strong-read units.

options.text: 48 RCUs
options.why: This is the corresponding strong-read rate, not eventual.

options.text: 96 RCUs
options.why: This is the corresponding transactional-read rate, not eventual.

review.analogy: Three cartons per item, half-price reads, sixteen orders per second.

review.title: Query vs Parallel Scan
review.question: A one-off export needs all items, no suitable key access exists, and spare read capacity is available. What can reduce elapsed scan time?

options.text: Query with only a FilterExpression
options.why: Query still requires partition-key equality; a filter cannot supply it.

options.text: Parallel Scan with paginated segment workers
options.why: Concurrent logical segments can reduce time, while consuming capacity and requiring per-worker pagination.

options.text: ProjectionExpression makes the scan free
options.why: Projection reduces returned fields, not Scan read capacity.

review.analogy: Several clerks can inspect separate filing-room sections, but each still reads the files.

review.title: Stateful vs stateless
review.question: HTTP reaches an ALB from Browser:54321, but the subnet outbound NACL allows only destination 80. What is missing?

options.text: Response destination ephemeral port
options.why: The response is ALB:80 → Browser:54321; the stateless NACL must allow that outbound destination.

options.text: A second inbound SG rule for source 80
options.why: SG tracking already permits the established response; the missing control is the NACL return path.

options.text: Change the browser source port to 80
options.why: Clients normally choose ephemeral source ports; the service destination is 80.

review.analogy: The return envelope is addressed to the caller’s temporary desk number.

review.title: Public frontend, private backend
review.question: Can an internet-facing ALB forward to an IP target in another VPC?

options.text: Only if the target has a public IP
options.why: Publicly routable IPs cannot be registered as ALB IP targets.

options.text: Registration alone makes it reachable
options.why: Registration creates no routing, security-group rules or return path.

options.text: Yes, for a supported private IP with working connectivity
options.why: Supported reachable private targets can be outside the VPC; routes, SGs, NACLs and health still apply.

review.analogy: A public reception desk can call a private office if a working connection exists.

review.title: Origins vs origin groups
review.question: An eligible GET must retry the same content from a backup after primary 503. What fits?

options.text: Multiple origins alone
options.why: They let behaviours route different requests; they do not automatically define a failover pair.

options.text: Origin group with configured failure conditions
options.why: The behaviour targets a primary/secondary pair. GET can fail over on configured errors.

options.text: Merge both origin responses
options.why: Origin groups retry; they do not combine responses.

review.analogy: Ask the backup shop for the same item, rather than combining two shopping baskets.

review.title: Dynamic delivery
review.question: /api/* returns dynamic JSON from an ALB. Does this alone require Lambda@Edge?

options.text: No; ordinary CloudFront origin delivery can handle it
options.why: Custom edge code is needed only when the request/response requires that custom processing.

options.text: Yes; every dynamic response requires edge code
options.why: Dynamic content and custom processing are separate responsibilities.

options.text: Use Global Accelerator to cache JSON
options.why: Global Accelerator is not a content cache.

review.analogy: Delivering a letter does not require rewriting it at every post office.

review.title: Shards vs replicas
review.question: Redis writes/storage need horizontal scaling across many well-distributed keys. What directly helps?

options.text: More replicas of the same shard
options.why: Replicas copy that shard and support reads/failover; they do not add independent primary write partitions.

options.text: Enable cluster mode without adding shards
options.why: The flag permits multi-shard topology, but does not itself add write capacity or replicas.

options.text: Add shards and distribute the keyspace
options.why: Each shard has a primary for its part of the keyspace; one hot key still maps to one shard.

review.analogy: Open another collection, rather than photocopying the same collection.

review.title: Queue encryption
review.question: A queue needs KMS encryption at rest with minimal application changes. Which fits?

options.text: SSE-KMS plus appropriate IAM/KMS permissions
options.why: SQS handles message encryption/decryption transparently for authorised clients.

options.text: Client-side encryption with no code changes
options.why: Client-side encryption needs application encryption and key-handling logic.

options.text: Secrets Manager encrypts queue storage
options.why: Secrets Manager stores secrets; SQS manages its own storage encryption.

review.analogy: The storage-room lock is managed by the queue, not installed by each visitor.

review.title: SSE-C and TLS
review.question: Who encrypts an SSE-C object, and how is the key supplied?

options.text: The client encrypts and never sends a key
options.why: That describes client-side encryption, not SSE-C.

options.text: S3 encrypts; client supplies the key over HTTPS
options.why: SSE-C is server-side. S3 requires HTTPS and does not persist the supplied key.

options.text: S3 retrieves the customer key from Secrets Manager automatically
options.why: That is not the SSE-C request model.

review.analogy: Lend the warehouse your key over a protected channel; it locks the box for you.

review.title: CodeDeploy lifecycle
review.question: Which sequence is correct for the core EC2 in-place lifecycle?

options.text: BeforeInstall → DownloadBundle → ApplicationStop
options.why: ApplicationStop and DownloadBundle precede BeforeInstall.

options.text: DownloadBundle → ApplicationStop → Install
options.why: ApplicationStop precedes the new bundle download and uses the prior successful revision.

options.text: ApplicationStop → DownloadBundle → BeforeInstall → Install → AfterInstall → ApplicationStart → ValidateService
options.why: This is the core order; DownloadBundle/Install are agent-reserved, and load-balanced deployments can add traffic events.

review.analogy: Stop → download → prepare → install → finish → start → test.

review.title: CodeCommit HTTPS
review.question: An IAM user needs a direct username/password for Git HTTPS to CodeCommit. What should they use?

options.text: IAM-generated CodeCommit Git credentials
options.why: These are service-specific Git credentials; a supported AWS credential helper is another approach.

options.text: AWS access key ID and secret as the raw Git login
options.why: Those are not the direct Git HTTPS username/password.

options.text: GitHub PAT after git login
options.why: A GitHub PAT authenticates GitHub, and Git has no standard git login command.

review.analogy: Use the badge issued for this repository host.

review.title: CloudFormation context
review.question: How should a template obtain its deployment Region without user input?

options.text: Declare AWS::Region as a String parameter
options.why: It is a built-in pseudo parameter, not a user parameter declaration.

options.text: !Ref AWS::Region
options.why: CloudFormation resolves AWS-provided deployment context; CDK can leave it as an unresolved token during synthesis.

options.text: Hard-code it as a universal compile-time constant
options.why: The deployment context can vary; hard-coding defeats reusable templates.

review.analogy: The office supplies its own address when processing your form.

review.title: API cache refresh
review.question: Which requests REST API entry invalidation when authorised and correctly configured?

options.text: ?bypass_cache=1
options.why: This query parameter has no built-in API Gateway invalidation meaning.

options.text: Bypass-Cache: 1
options.why: This is not the required invalidation header.

options.text: Cache-Control: max-age=0
options.why: With required execute-api:InvalidateCache permission and configuration, fetch a fresh backend response and update the entry.

review.analogy: An authorised check-again instruction replaces the cached order slip.

review.title: Detailed vs custom
review.question: An EC2 application must scale on memory utilisation. What is needed?

options.text: Only enable detailed monitoring
options.why: Detailed monitoring increases native frequency; it does not add guest memory metrics.

options.text: CloudWatch Agent or another custom memory publisher
options.why: Publish guest memory, then configure the appropriate alarm/scaling policy.

options.text: ALB RequestCount without an ALB
options.why: No ALB means no such metric; requests also do not directly measure memory.

review.analogy: A faster speedometer does not become a fuel gauge.

review.title: Identity vs resource policy
review.question: SNS must send to one SQS queue. Where is the queue access grant normally expressed?

options.text: Queue policy: Principal sns.amazonaws.com, sqs:SendMessage, restricted source topic
options.why: A queue resource policy grants the service principal access; add relevant KMS permissions for SSE-KMS.

options.text: An “SQS role” trust policy
options.why: A queue policy is not a role trust policy, and SQS has no special identity type called an SQS role.

options.text: A permissions boundary by itself
options.why: A boundary restricts permissions; it does not independently grant them.

review.analogy: Put the named delivery service on the room’s guest list.

review3.title: DAX vs general cache
review3.question: A product catalogue repeats eventual DynamoDB reads and wants minimal custom cache population/invalidation code. Which fits best?

options.text: DAX with a compatible client/endpoint
options.why: DAX manages the eligible item/query cache path. Results can be shared by clients using the same relevant keys/queries.

options.text: Redis because it cannot cache DynamoDB otherwise
options.why: Redis absolutely can cache DynamoDB; it needs application-managed cache logic, so the stated reason is false.

options.text: CloudFront as a direct DynamoDB SDK cache
options.why: CloudFront caches HTTP representations, not native DynamoDB SDK operations.

review3.analogy: Use a DynamoDB-aware librarian rather than organising every cache shelf yourself.

review3.title: Strong reads and DAX
review3.question: A DAX client requests ConsistentRead=true on a supported table read. What should you expect?

options.text: A strong read served from the DAX cache
options.why: DAX cache hits are eventually consistent; this would misstate the guarantee.

options.text: DAX forwards the read to DynamoDB without caching that strong result
options.why: The strong consistency requirement is met by DynamoDB, not by a DAX cache hit.

options.text: DAX converts it to an eventual GSI read
options.why: DAX does not change the requirement into a GSI read; GSIs cannot serve strong reads.

review3.analogy: Go to the original signed ledger when the latest committed entry is required.

review3.title: Which permission direction?
review3.question: API Gateway accepts a caller but fails before a Lambda function executes. Adding DynamoDB access to the Lambda role did not help. What should you inspect?

options.text: Only the Lambda execution role
options.why: That role controls outgoing AWS calls after the function runs.

options.text: The client’s Redis session TTL
options.why: It does not grant the API Gateway integration permission to invoke Lambda.

options.text: The selected integration target and API Gateway invocation permission
options.why: Check the function/alias resource policy or correctly configured invocation role. Missing permission can cause HTTP 500.

review3.analogy: The receptionist needs permission to call the office before the office can open its filing cabinet.

review3.title: STS vs authorisation
review3.question: A client assumes an IAM role, then calls an AWS_IAM-protected API. What authorises the incoming request?

options.text: API Gateway treats STS as a built-in authoriser
options.why: STS supplies credentials; it is not a standalone API Gateway authoriser.

options.text: IAM evaluation of a properly signed request using the temporary credentials
options.why: The client uses the STS-issued key/session credentials to sign, normally with SigV4, and needs execute-api:Invoke.

options.text: Lambda’s execution role authenticates the client
options.why: That role controls the function’s downstream AWS permissions, not incoming API caller authorisation.

review3.analogy: STS issues the badge; the API checks the badge and its permitted access.

review3.title: Stage variable vs grant
review3.question: dev defines lambdaFunction=my-api-dev and prod defines my-api-prod. What does the variable itself provide?

options.text: Configuration selecting the integration target
options.why: Stages hold key/value settings; the integration can interpolate a function/alias, which still needs invocation permission.

options.text: lambda:InvokeFunction permission on both functions
options.why: A configuration value is not a policy grant.

options.text: A new Lambda execution role for every call
options.why: Variables do not provision execution roles or isolate application state automatically.

review3.analogy: Changing the office number in a directory does not give you an access badge.

review3.title: Projection vs filtering
review3.question: A Users Scan should return Name/Email only, and only active users. Which description is correct?

options.text: Projection filters rows and filter selects columns
options.why: Those responsibilities are reversed.

options.text: Projection/filter reduce read capacity for the same evaluated items
options.why: They reduce output, not the underlying read capacity for evaluating those items.

options.text: Projection chooses attributes; filter removes non-matching items after reading
options.why: Use expression aliases where needed. A suitable key/index can avoid a full Scan; output filters alone do not.

review3.analogy: Choose spreadsheet columns separately from which rows remain visible.

review3.title: FIFO group boundary
review3.question: Two users’ purchases need per-user order, with different users processing concurrently. What should the producer set?

options.text: MessageGroupId=user_id
options.why: Same-group order is preserved; different groups can progress concurrently.

options.text: One shared group for every user
options.why: This serialises all users into one ordering boundary instead of permitting cross-user group parallelism.

options.text: MessageOrderId=user_id
options.why: MessageOrderId is not an SQS SendMessage parameter.

review3.analogy: One checkout lane per ordering group, rather than one lane for the whole store.

review3.title: Deduplication does not delete
review3.question: A FIFO message was processed and deleted. The producer retries the same logical MessageDeduplicationId two minutes after the first send. What occurs?

options.text: SQS deletes any newer queued message
options.why: Deduplication suppresses the duplicate send; it is not a delete request.

options.text: The retry can be acknowledged without a new deliverable message
options.why: Deduplication history persists for the five-minute window even after the original message is deleted.

options.text: A new message must be delivered because the first was deleted
options.why: Deletion does not automatically remove the send-deduplication history.

review3.analogy: A used receipt number remains recognised after the original order is collected.

review3.title: Declared vs packaged dependency
review3.question: A Lambda ZIP contains index.js and package.json listing pg, but no installed pg code or dependency layer. What is missing?

options.text: Lambda must be told to run npm install at each cold start
options.why: ZIP deployment does not automatically install npm dependencies; build/install before deployment.

options.text: A bigger memory setting
options.why: More CPU/memory does not supply the missing module files.

options.text: Installed/bundled dependencies in the artifact or a configured layer
options.why: Run npm ci/install at build time; include required runtime code and correct archive paths.

review3.analogy: A shopping list is not the ingredients in the pantry.

review3.title: Index write back-pressure
review3.question: One hundred new items/s each require a 1.5 KB GSI entry. The GSI has 150 WCUs; table capacity is ample. What is the concern?

options.text: The GSI needs 200 WCUs before headroom and can back-pressure base writes
options.why: ceil(1.5/1) × 100 = 200 index WCUs. Its insufficient write budget can throttle associated table writes.

options.text: The GSI can borrow spare base-table WCUs automatically
options.why: Provisioned GSI capacity is separate, unlike LSI capacity.

options.text: Only GSI queries can throttle; base writes are unaffected
options.why: An under-provisioned GSI write path can throttle base-table writes.

review3.analogy: A fast factory can still back up when its required indexing desk cannot keep pace.

review3.title: Index read budget
review3.question: A GSI Query retrieves one projected 12 KB entry per request at 16 requests/s. What eventual read budget applies before headroom?

options.text: 48 base-table RCUs
options.why: That is strong-read arithmetic; GSI queries use their own eventual-read capacity.

options.text: 24 GSI RCUs
options.why: ceil(12/4) × 0.5 × 16 = 24 RCUs on the index. This example has one returned/evaluated entry per Query.

options.text: No read cost because the table was already indexed
options.why: A GSI has its own reads, storage and affected-write costs.

review3.analogy: Pay the separate catalogue’s read desk at the eventual-read rate.

review3.title: Stable-IP cutover
review3.question: A replacement must preserve the public IPv4 of an EC2-hosted service. Which approach fits, with the right caveat?

options.text: Route 53 automatically preserves the EC2 public IP
options.why: DNS answers can point to addresses; failover does not make a new instance inherit an old address.

options.text: Stopping the old server guarantees zero downtime
options.why: A period without a ready serving instance is disruptive.

options.text: Prepare/test the replacement, then reassociate the EIP in its Region
options.why: The IP stays stable, but reassociation and connection recovery can briefly interrupt traffic.

review3.analogy: Keep the phone number while transferring it to a prepared office; calls can still drop.

review3.title: Query string cache key
review3.question: The origin returns the requested review language, but CloudFront serves English for lang=jp after caching lang=en. What should change?

options.text: Include lang in the cache key and ensure it reaches the origin
options.why: Different representations need distinct keys; origin-request forwarding alone does not distinguish cached objects.

options.text: Only reduce TTL
options.why: A shorter TTL does not make a key that ignores language correct.

options.text: Replace the query parameter with an unrelated header automatically
options.why: Headers and query parameters are different inputs; a matching cache/origin design is still required.

review3.analogy: Translated folders need language labels, not just a faster replacement schedule.

review3.title: Historical CodeStar clue
review3.question: An older question describes a unified AWS development project dashboard. What is the accurate modern reading?

options.text: CodeStar is the recommended new dashboard today
options.why: The original CodeStar project capability retired in July 2024.

options.text: The old clue may mean CodeStar; use current CI/CD tools for current designs
options.why: CodeBuild builds/tests, CodeDeploy deploys and CodePipeline orchestrates. CodeConnections is a separate capability.

options.text: CodeConnections retired with the CodeStar dashboard
options.why: The old CodeStar Connections name does not imply the separate connection service was retired.

review3.analogy: Recognise the old control-room name without trying to open a retired control room.

review3.title: KCL shard leases
review3.question: One KCL application has 10 shards and 20 one-worker EC2 instances. What is the settled shard-level allocation limit?

options.text: Twenty workers each get half a shard lease
options.why: The basic lease-processing model assigns a shard to one active worker within an application.

options.text: Only one worker can read the entire stream
options.why: One worker can own multiple shards, but multiple workers can own different shards.

options.text: At most 10 workers do shard-level processing; the others have no shard lease
options.why: More workers do not create more shards. Independent consumer applications have separate ownership sets.

review3.analogy: Twenty clerks cannot create twenty checkout lanes in a ten-lane store.

review3.title: Data-key request reduction
review3.question: An illustrative single-client model encrypts 1,000 matching-context messages, with 100 uses per cached data key and no earlier age/byte expiry. About how many fresh data-key calls occur?

options.why: ceil(1000/100) = 10 in this simple model. Actual SDK thresholds, misses and contexts can refresh sooner.

options.text: 1,000 regardless of eligible caching
options.why: Fresh-per-message would need approximately 1,000; eligible bounded caching is intended to reduce those requests.

options.text: Zero because KMS stores the client cache
options.why: A fresh key still needs initial materials; the application/SDK cache is not automatically stored by KMS.

review3.analogy: A bounded batch reuses a protected work key, then requests a fresh one.

review3.title: Data-key caching safety
review3.question: Eligible data-key caching is enabled. Which assumption remains unsafe?

options.text: Age, message and byte thresholds can limit reuse
options.why: Those are useful security boundaries, along with supported algorithm/context handling.

options.text: The same key means an IV/nonce may be reused for every encryption
options.why: Key reuse does not permit nonce/IV reuse. Follow the SDK’s cryptographic construction and protect cached materials.

options.text: S3 Bucket Keys are specific to S3 SSE-KMS
options.why: Correct: they are not an arbitrary application-transaction data-key cache.

review3.analogy: Reusing a protected work key is not reusing the same per-message seal.

review3.title: TTL does not refresh
review3.question: Popular profiles tolerate up to 60 seconds of staleness and cache space is limited. What fits, and what happens at expiry?

options.text: Write every profile into cache; expiry proactively queries the DB
options.why: That caches never-read profiles, and ordinary TTL expiry does not automatically fetch the source.

options.text: Lazy loading without TTL guarantees the 60-second bound
options.why: Without expiry/invalidation, a cache-aside entry can remain stale much longer.

options.text: Lazy loading + TTL; the next read after expiry fetches/populates
options.why: Only requested items are cached, with an expiry boundary; real concurrency/failures still need consideration.

review3.analogy: The use-by label invalidates the shelf copy; a customer’s next request restocks it.

review3.title: Update vs delete cache
review3.question: After committing a new product price, the app should avoid maintaining the new cached representation. Which pattern fits?

options.text: Delete the cache entry after the DB write; next read repopulates
options.why: Write-invalidate differs from write-through, which sets the updated cached representation. Handle deletion failure and read/write races.

options.text: Call TTL and assume it updates the cached price immediately
options.why: TTL expiration does not write a new cached value or guarantee an immediate refresh.

options.text: Use two ordinary writes as an atomic DB/cache transaction
options.why: Separate DB/cache calls are not automatically atomic; strict freshness needs stronger controls.

review3.analogy: Remove the old price card; the next reader fetches the new one.

review3.title: Gateway route vs interface ENI
review3.question: Private EC2 needs ordinary same-VPC DynamoDB access without NAT and with minimal endpoint cost. Which statement fits?

options.text: DynamoDB supports only interface endpoints
options.why: It supports gateway and interface endpoints.

options.text: A gateway endpoint uses a prefix-list route; a DynamoDB interface endpoint is also supported for other needs
options.why: Gateway access needs the route-table association, no endpoint ENI/SG, and no additional endpoint charge.

options.text: A gateway endpoint always resolves to a new private ENI IP
options.why: That describes the interface-endpoint mechanism, not a gateway route.

review3.analogy: Change a route sign for a gateway; build a private-IP entrance for an interface endpoint.

review3.title: Role detachment and bucket access
review3.question: An EC2 role was detached and its old credentials expired. Reads still work through a bucket policy explicitly allowing anonymous GetObject, with BPA permitting it. Why?

options.text: S3 gives a five-minute read grace period
options.why: There is no special five-minute read grace period.

options.text: The expired role credentials still authorise signed requests forever
options.why: Expired credentials do not provide a valid authenticated role identity.

options.text: The anonymous request has a separate applicable resource-policy grant
options.why: The scenario explicitly permits public reads. Named-principal bucket grants would still need matching valid credentials; other controls can deny.

review3.analogy: Closing the badge dispenser does not close a separately permitted public doorway.

review3.title: CLI output pages
review3.question: A 250-object listing uses --max-items 100. How does the caller obtain the next output page?

options.text: Pass the prior CLI NextToken unchanged as --starting-token
options.why: This yields the next output page: 100, 100, then 50 objects in the fixed dataset. --page-size controls underlying calls.

options.text: Pass --next-token as the generic CLI paginator input
options.why: That is not the corresponding CLI input; command-specific service tokens are a separate concept.

options.text: Set --page-size 100 and expect it to stop total output at 100
options.why: Page size controls each service call, not the complete automatically paginated output.

review3.analogy: The clerk’s claim ticket resumes your output pile; box size controls warehouse deliveries.

review3.title: Searchable trace data
review3.question: Traces must be searchable by tenant, with a nested debugging payload retained for inspection. Where should each go?

options.text: Tenant in metadata; nested object in an annotation
options.why: Metadata is not indexed, and annotations are scalar indexed values.

options.text: Tenant annotation; nested object in metadata
options.why: Use an annotation filter to find traces, then inspect non-indexed metadata. Segments describe service work, not infrastructure stacks.

options.text: Put both in the sampling rate
options.why: Sampling controls whether requests are traced, not their indexed business labels.

review3.analogy: Use an indexed parcel label to find the package; read the detailed note inside it.

review3.title: Worker scheduling
review3.question: A Beanstalk app must enqueue hourly video jobs for its worker HTTP endpoint. What is the native scheduling path?

options.text: A web-tier package.json cron field creates scheduled SQS messages
options.why: That is not the Beanstalk native scheduled-worker mechanism.

options.text: .ebextensions is the recurring-job schedule file
options.why: It configures/provisions the environment; it is not cron.yaml.

options.text: Worker-tier cron.yaml → scheduler → SQS → daemon → application POST
options.why: The scheduler enqueues; the daemon delivers work to the local application endpoint. Jobs still need retry/idempotency handling.

review3.analogy: The timetable creates a ticket, the queue holds it, and the worker delivers it to the back office.

review3.title: Actual key vs key identifier
review3.question: The customer sends an actual encryption key to S3 over HTTPS; S3 encrypts and does not persist that key. Which mode is this?

options.text: SSE-C; it does not inherently require KMS
options.why: S3 performs the cryptography with the supplied key. SSE-KMS instead uses KMS-protected data keys and normally a key identifier, not customer plaintext key material.

options.text: SSE-KMS because all customer keys require KMS import
options.why: Importing key material into KMS is separate from supplying an SSE-C key.

options.text: Client-side encryption because the customer owns the key
options.why: Client-side means encryption happens before upload; in this scenario S3 encrypts.

review3.analogy: Lend the warehouse your key to lock the box; you have not delivered an already encrypted box.
